The Working Class, also known as the Proletariat. People who earn wages by selling their labor rather than owning productive capital—factory workers, miners, farmhands, and service workers whose collective muscle and skill powered the Industrial Revolution and modern economies. Defined socially by their economic dependence and subordination to employers, the working class became the revolutionary agent in Marxist theory and the political base of labor movements and socialist parties throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Though materially better-off in wealthy nations today, class divisions remain fundamental to how wealth, power, and culture are distributed.

The working class emerged as a distinct class during industrialization. Enclosure movements displaced peasants, driving mass migration to factory towns where workers sold labor by the hour. They worked in dangerous, unsanitary conditions for subsistence wages. Child labor, twelve-hour shifts, and industrial injuries were routine until reform movements intervened.

Workers developed collective consciousness through the labor movement—trade unions, strikes, and political organizing gave workers bargaining power against employers. Karl Marx theorized that capitalist exploitation of workers would inevitably generate class conflict and revolution, with the working class as history's liberating force.

The working class differed from the historical peasantry. Industrial workers were atomized, concentrated in cities, and dependent on cash wages rather than land. They supported the rise of socialist and communist parties, such as the Labour Party in Britain, that explicitly claimed to represent working-class interests.

Working-class communities developed distinct cultural identities—dialects, music, literature, and values—from jazz in New Orleans to punk rock in nineteen seventies London. The working class was created by the capitalist system that appropriates its surplus labor, yet the labor movement and socialist ideology gave workers a voice and collective power in the modern world.
